title: Ester + 2 RMgX → 3° alcohol (adds twice)
reagentDisplay: 1. CH3MgBr (2 equiv or excess), ether  2. H3O+

steps.label: The first CH3MgBr adds to the ester carbonyl carbon
steps.note: The C–Mg bond acts like CH3⁻; the C=O π electrons move onto oxygen.

steps.label: The tetrahedral intermediate collapses: C=O reforms and methoxide leaves
steps.note: The product of the first addition is a ketone, which is more reactive than the ester.

steps.label: A second CH3MgBr adds to the ketone carbonyl carbon
steps.note: The ketone can't be stopped at: it reacts faster than the remaining ester, so two R groups add.

steps.label: Acid workup protonates the alkoxide

why: The first methyl adds and methoxide leaves (add, then eliminate), giving a ketone. That ketone is more reactive than the starting ester, so a second equivalent adds right away. Two identical R groups end up on the old carbonyl carbon.

traps.explains: The ketone does form, but it's more reactive than the ester and the Grignard is still there, so it doesn't stop. To stop at a ketone, use R2CuLi with an acid chloride.
This tetrahedral intermediate doesn't survive. An ester carbon has a leaving group (methoxide), so it collapses back to C=O.
This has only one new methyl and an extra H. Grignards deliver carbon, not hydride, and they add twice to esters.

title: Carboxylic acid + SOCl2 → acid chloride

steps.label: The acid's OH oxygen attacks sulfur; the S=O π electrons move onto oxygen
steps.note: SOCl2 is attacked at sulfur first, turning the OH into a far better leaving group.

steps.label: S=O reforms and a chloride ion is expelled from sulfur
A chloride ion removes the proton from the oxonium oxygen, giving the acyl chlorosulfite
steps.note: HCl gas is released.

steps.label: Chloride attacks the carbonyl carbon of the acyl chlorosulfite
C=O reforms and the chlorosulfite leaves, falling apart into SO2 and Cl⁻
steps.note: SO2 and HCl leave as gases, which drives the reaction to completion.

why: You normally can't climb the reactivity ladder (acid chloride > anhydride > ester ≈ acid > amide), but SOCl2 first turns the OH into a chlorosulfite, an excellent leaving group. Chloride then attacks the acyl carbon and the leaving group falls apart into SO2 and Cl⁻, so the reaction is driven by loss of SO2 gas.

traps.explains: No reaction is the wrong call. Direct substitution can't go up the ladder, but SOCl2 activates the OH (chlorosulfite) so chloride can displace it.
SOCl2 swaps only the OH for Cl; the C=O stays. Turning C–OH into C–Cl with loss of the carbonyl is not what happens (alcohols give alkyl chlorides, acids give acid chlorides).
This acyl chlorosulfite is the activated intermediate. It doesn't survive: chloride attacks the acyl carbon and SO2 + Cl⁻ leave.

title: Acid chloride + H2O → carboxylic acid

steps.label: Water attacks the carbonyl carbon
The tetrahedral intermediate collapses: C=O reforms and chloride leaves
steps.note: Cl⁻ is an excellent leaving group, which is why acid chlorides react even with water.

steps.label: Water removes the proton from the protonated acid

why: Acid chlorides are at the top of the reactivity ladder, so even water, a weak nucleophile, adds to the C=O carbon. The tetrahedral intermediate collapses, chloride (a great leaving group) leaves, and HCl is the byproduct.

traps.explains: This is the tetrahedral intermediate. It collapses back to C=O and expels chloride, the best leaving group on that carbon.
No base is present. The reaction releases HCl, so the solution is acidic and the acid stays protonated.
An anhydride forms from an acid chloride plus a carboxylate. Here water is the nucleophile, so you simply get the acid.

title: Acid chloride + alcohol (pyridine) → ester

steps.label: The alcohol oxygen attacks the carbonyl carbon
The tetrahedral intermediate collapses: C=O reforms and chloride leaves
Pyridine removes the proton from the oxonium oxygen
steps.note: Pyridine soaks up the HCl so it can't build up and protonate things.

why: The alcohol oxygen attacks the very reactive acid chloride carbonyl, and chloride leaves: a step down the reactivity ladder from acid chloride to ester. Pyridine is a weak base that soaks up the HCl formed.

traps.explains: That's hydrolysis by water. Here the nucleophile is the ethanol oxygen, so the ethoxy group ends up on the carbonyl.
The alcohol bonds through its oxygen, not through carbon, so no ketone forms. Making a ketone from an acid chloride needs a carbon nucleophile such as R2CuLi.
Acyl substitution keeps the C=O; only the chlorine is replaced. The carbonyl oxygen does not leave to give an ether.

title: Acid chloride + 2 amine → amide

steps.label: The amine nitrogen attacks the carbonyl carbon
The tetrahedral intermediate collapses: C=O reforms and chloride leaves
A second molecule of amine removes the proton from nitrogen
steps.note: This is why 2 equivalents of amine are needed: the second one ends up as CH3NH3⁺ Cl⁻.

why: The amine nitrogen attacks the acid chloride and chloride leaves, going down the ladder to the most stable derivative, the amide. The HCl formed would protonate the amine and make it non-nucleophilic, so a second equivalent of amine is added just to mop up the HCl as CH3NH3⁺ Cl⁻.

traps.explains: This salt does form, but it's the byproduct: the second equivalent of amine acting as a base to trap HCl. The organic product is the amide.
The amide N doesn't react again: its lone pair is delocalized into the C=O, so it is not nucleophilic enough. The second equivalent of amine is only a base.
Acyl substitution keeps the C=O. Turning an amide into an amine needs a reduction (LiAlH4).

title: Acid chloride + carboxylate → anhydride

steps.label: The carboxylate oxygen attacks the carbonyl carbon
The tetrahedral intermediate collapses: C=O reforms and chloride leaves
steps.note: The carboxylate is already anionic, so no proton transfer is needed at the end.

why: The negatively charged carboxylate oxygen attacks the acid chloride carbonyl and chloride leaves. Acid chloride → anhydride is one step down the reactivity ladder, so it goes readily.

traps.explains: There's no water here. The carboxylate is the nucleophile and stays bonded to the acyl carbon, giving an anhydride rather than just being protonated.
This tetrahedral intermediate collapses: the C=O re-forms and chloride, the best leaving group, is expelled.
A carboxylate is an oxygen nucleophile, not a carbon nucleophile, so no C–C bond forms. A ketone from an acid chloride needs R2CuLi.

title: Fischer esterification (acid + alcohol, H+)

steps.label: Acid protonates the carbonyl oxygen
steps.note: Protonation makes the carbonyl carbon much more electrophilic, so a weak nucleophile (CH3OH) can attack.

steps.label: Methanol attacks the protonated carbonyl carbon
Methanol removes the proton from the added oxygen
Acid protonates one OH group, turning it into a good leaving group
steps.note: Either OH can be protonated; protonating the original OH leads on to the ester.

steps.label: Water leaves as the remaining OH reforms the C=O
Methanol removes the proton from the carbonyl oxygen, giving the ester and regenerating the acid catalyst
steps.note: Every step is reversible; excess methanol (and removing water) pushes the equilibrium to the ester.

why: Acid protonates the C=O, making the carbonyl carbon electrophilic enough for neutral methanol to attack; after proton transfers, water leaves. Acid and ester sit at about the same level on the ladder, so every step is reversible: use excess alcohol or remove water to push it to the ester.

traps.explains: It does react. Acid ≈ ester on the ladder, so it is an equilibrium, and excess methanol (or removing water) drives it toward the ester.
This is the tetrahedral intermediate. After a proton transfer it loses water and the C=O re-forms.
Two acids don't condense to an anhydride under these conditions. Methanol is present in excess and is the nucleophile.

title: Ester + H3O+ → carboxylic acid (acid hydrolysis)

steps.label: Acid protonates the carbonyl oxygen
Water attacks the protonated carbonyl carbon
Water removes a proton from the added oxygen
Acid protonates the OCH2CH3 oxygen, turning it into a good leaving group
Ethanol leaves as an OH reforms the C=O
Water removes the proton from the carbonyl oxygen, giving the acid and regenerating H3O⁺
steps.note: This is Fischer esterification run backwards; a large excess of water drives it toward the acid.

why: This is Fischer esterification run backwards: acid protonates the C=O, water attacks, and ethanol leaves after proton transfers. Every step is reversible, so a large excess of water is used to push the equilibrium toward the acid + alcohol.

traps.explains: The carboxylate is what base (saponification) gives. In acid the product stays protonated as the carboxylic acid.
It is an equilibrium, but with a large excess of water and heat it shifts to acid + alcohol. To make the ester you'd use excess alcohol instead (Fischer).
This is the tetrahedral intermediate. It loses ethanol (after a proton transfer) and the C=O re-forms.

title: Saponification: ester + NaOH → acid (after workup)

steps.label: Hydroxide attacks the ester carbonyl carbon
The tetrahedral intermediate collapses: C=O reforms and methoxide leaves
Methoxide removes the acidic proton from the carboxylic acid
steps.note: This acid–base step is essentially irreversible, which is why saponification goes to completion.

steps.label: Acid workup protonates the carboxylate

why: Hydroxide attacks the ester carbonyl and methoxide leaves. The acid formed is immediately deprotonated to the carboxylate, which is negatively charged and no longer electrophilic, so unlike acid hydrolysis this is irreversible. Step 2 (H3O+) protonates the carboxylate to give the carboxylic acid.

traps.explains: Sodium benzoate is what's in the flask after step 1. The H3O+ workup in step 2 protonates it to benzoic acid.
Hydroxide is a nucleophile, not a hydride source. Reducing an ester to a 1° alcohol needs LiAlH4.
This tetrahedral intermediate collapses: the C=O re-forms and methoxide leaves.

title: Amide + H3O+, heat → carboxylic acid

steps.label: Acid protonates the carbonyl oxygen
steps.note: The carbonyl O, not the N, is protonated: the N lone pair is tied up in resonance with C=O.

steps.label: Water attacks the protonated carbonyl carbon
Water removes a proton from the added oxygen
Acid protonates the nitrogen, turning NH2 into a leaving group
steps.note: Once the C=O is gone the nitrogen is an ordinary amine, the most basic site.

steps.label: NH3 leaves as an OH reforms the C=O
Water removes the proton from the carbonyl oxygen, giving the carboxylic acid
steps.note: The NH3 released is protonated to NH4⁺ in the acid, so it can't attack back: that makes the hydrolysis irreversible.

why: Amides are at the bottom of the reactivity ladder, so hydrolysis needs strong acid (or base) and prolonged heating. In acid, water attacks the protonated carbonyl and NH3 leaves; it is trapped as NH4⁺, which makes the reaction irreversible. Hot NaOH also works, giving the carboxylate (acid after H3O+ workup) and NH3.

traps.explains: That's LiAlH4 reduction of the amide (C=O → CH2). Hot aqueous acid hydrolyzes the C–N bond instead.
The carboxylate is what basic hydrolysis gives before acidification. In hot aqueous acid you get the carboxylic acid and NH4⁺.
Dehydrating a 1° amide (SOCl2 or P2O5) gives a nitrile. Here water is added, not removed.

title: Nitrile + H3O+, heat → carboxylic acid

steps.label: Acid protonates the nitrile nitrogen
Water attacks the nitrile carbon
Water removes a proton from the added oxygen, giving an imidic acid
Acid protonates the imidic acid nitrogen
Water removes the O–H proton; C=O forms and the C=N π electrons move onto nitrogen, giving the amide
steps.note: Steps 4–5 are the imidic acid → amide tautomerization. The amide is then hydrolysed like any amide.

steps.label: Acid protonates the amide carbonyl oxygen
A second water attacks the protonated carbonyl carbon
Water removes a proton from the newly added oxygen
Acid protonates the nitrogen
NH3 leaves as an OH reforms the C=O
Water removes the proton from the carbonyl oxygen, giving the carboxylic acid
steps.note: NH3 is trapped as NH4⁺ in the acid, which pulls the whole sequence forward.

why: Acid protonates the nitrile N, and water adds to the nitrile carbon; tautomerization gives an amide. Under the hot aqueous acid the amide is hydrolyzed further, so the nitrile carbon ends up as a COOH and the nitrogen leaves as NH4⁺.

traps.explains: The amide is an intermediate. With heat and excess aqueous acid it is hydrolyzed on to the carboxylic acid.
That's LiAlH4 reduction of the nitrile. Water adds O to the nitrile carbon; nothing delivers hydride.
The carboxylate comes from basic hydrolysis (before acidification). In hot aqueous acid you get the neutral carboxylic acid.

title: Nitrile + RMgX → ketone (adds once)

steps.label: CH3MgBr adds to the nitrile carbon, giving an imine anion
steps.note: The negatively charged imine salt can't be attacked again, so only one R group adds.

steps.label: Workup: acid protonates the imine anion nitrogen
Acid protonates the imine nitrogen, giving an iminium ion
steps.note: From here on this is imine hydrolysis.

steps.label: Water attacks the iminium carbon
Water removes a proton from the added oxygen
Acid protonates the nitrogen, turning NH2 into a leaving group
NH3 leaves as the OH reforms a C=O
Water removes the proton from the carbonyl oxygen, giving the ketone

why: The Grignard carbon adds once to the nitrile carbon, giving a negatively charged imine salt (C=N⁻ MgBr⁺) that won't accept a second Grignard. Aqueous acid workup then hydrolyzes the imine to a ketone, so unlike an ester, a nitrile stops at the ketone.

traps.explains: That's the ester result (adds twice). The nitrile gives an imine anion that is already negatively charged, so a second Grignard doesn't add.
The imine forms after protonation, but aqueous acid workup hydrolyzes it to the ketone.
That's nitrile hydrolysis (H3O+, heat). The Grignard first adds a carbon, so the product has a new C–C bond.

distractors.explains: An ester doesn't stop at the ketone: the ketone is more reactive than the ester, so a second CH3MgBr adds and you get the 3° alcohol.
An aldehyde has no leaving group, so the Grignard just adds and you get the 2° alcohol, 1-phenylethanol, not the ketone.

title: Nitrile + LiAlH4 → 1° amine

steps.label: Hydride from AlH4⁻ adds to the nitrile carbon
A second hydride adds to the imine anion carbon
steps.note: Unlike the Grignard case, the small hydride adds a second time, giving a dianion (really held by aluminum).

steps.label: Workup: water protonates the nitrogen
A second water protonates the nitrogen, giving the primary amine

why: Hydride adds to the nitrile carbon to give an imine anion; LiAlH4 is strong enough to add a second hydride to that C=N. Water workup protonates the nitrogen, so the C≡N becomes CH2–NH2 with no carbons gained or lost.

traps.explains: DIBAL-H adds one hydride and the imine is hydrolyzed to an aldehyde. LiAlH4 adds a second hydride, so the nitrogen is kept as an amine.
The imine (anion) is an intermediate. LiAlH4 adds a second hydride to the C=N.
That's nitrile hydrolysis (H3O+, heat). LiAlH4 is a reducing agent: it adds H, not O.

title: Ester + LiAlH4 → 1° alcohol

steps.label: Hydride from AlH4⁻ adds to the ester carbonyl carbon
The tetrahedral intermediate collapses: C=O reforms and ethoxide leaves
steps.note: The aldehyde formed is more reactive than the ester, so it can't be isolated with LiAlH4.

steps.label: A second hydride adds to the aldehyde carbonyl carbon
Acid workup protonates the alkoxide

why: Hydride adds and ethoxide leaves, giving an aldehyde. The aldehyde is more reactive than the ester, so a second hydride adds at once, and workup gives a 1° alcohol (plus the ethanol that left).

traps.explains: LiAlH4 doesn't stop at the aldehyde: the aldehyde is more reactive than the ester and gets reduced again. DIBAL-H at −78 °C does stop there.
No reaction would be NaBH4, which is too weak to reduce esters. LiAlH4 is strong enough.
The ethoxy group leaves after the first hydride adds; it isn't kept. The C=O carbon ends up as CH2OH.

title: Ester + DIBAL-H (−78 °C) → aldehyde

steps.label: The carbonyl oxygen coordinates to aluminum (Lewis acid–base)
steps.note: DIBAL-H is neutral and Lewis acidic; binding to Al activates the C=O.

steps.label: Hydride is delivered from aluminum to the carbonyl carbon
steps.note: At −78 °C this aluminum-bound tetrahedral intermediate is stable, so it does not collapse and no second hydride adds.

steps.label: Aqueous workup: water attacks aluminum and frees the alkoxide oxygen
The tetrahedral intermediate collapses: C=O reforms and methoxide leaves
steps.note: By the time the aldehyde forms, the DIBAL has been destroyed by the water, so it survives.

why: DIBAL-H delivers only one hydride, and at −78 °C the tetrahedral aluminum intermediate is stable and doesn't collapse. It only breaks down to the aldehyde during aqueous workup, when no hydride is left to reduce it further.

traps.explains: Over-reduction to the 1° alcohol is what LiAlH4 gives (or DIBAL if warmed or in excess). One equivalent at −78 °C stops at the aldehyde.
The hemiacetal is the intermediate held at −78 °C (as its Al salt). On aqueous workup it collapses to the aldehyde and methanol.
DIBAL-H is a reducing agent; it adds hydride, not hydroxide. Ester → acid is hydrolysis (H3O+ or NaOH).

title: Acid chloride + LiAlH(OtBu)3 → aldehyde

steps.label: LiAlH(OtBu)3 delivers a hydride to the acid chloride carbonyl carbon
steps.note: The bulky, weak hydride donor has only one H, and it reacts with the very reactive acid chloride faster than with the aldehyde.

steps.label: The tetrahedral intermediate collapses: C=O reforms and chloride leaves

why: LiAlH(OtBu)3 is a bulky, mild hydride with only one H to give. It reduces the very reactive acid chloride (chloride leaves) but reacts only slowly with the less reactive aldehyde product, especially at low temperature, so it stops at the aldehyde.

traps.explains: LiAlH4 would reduce the acid chloride all the way to the 1° alcohol. The bulky, weaker LiAlH(OtBu)3 stops at the aldehyde.
The tert-butoxy groups stay on aluminum. The reagent transfers hydride, so no tert-butyl ester forms.
That's hydrolysis by water. The reagent's hydride is the nucleophile, so the C–Cl becomes C–H.

title: Amide + LiAlH4 → amine

steps.label: Hydride from AlH4⁻ adds to the amide carbonyl carbon
The alkoxide oxygen bonds to aluminum (AlH3), making it a leaving group
steps.note: Oxygen bound to aluminum leaves far more easily than a bare O²⁻ would.

steps.label: The nitrogen lone pair pushes out the O–Al group, forming an iminium ion
steps.note: Here N, the better electron donor, kicks out O: the opposite of what happens with esters, so the C–N bond survives.

steps.label: A second hydride adds to the iminium carbon, giving the amine

why: Hydride adds to the amide C=O, but then the oxygen (bound to aluminum) is lost instead of the nitrogen, giving an iminium ion. A second hydride reduces the iminium, so the C=O becomes CH2 and the C–N bond is kept: an amine, not an alcohol.

traps.explains: With an ester the OR leaves, but with an amide the oxygen leaves (as an Al–O species) and the nitrogen stays, so you get an amine, not an alcohol.
LiAlH4 doesn't stop partway. The intermediate iminium ion is reduced again, and the nitrogen is kept.
No reaction would be NaBH4, which can't reduce amides. LiAlH4 is strong enough.

title: Carboxylic acid + LiAlH4 → 1° alcohol

steps.label: Acid–base first: a hydride removes the acidic O–H proton, releasing H2
steps.note: LiAlH4 is a strong base, so the first equivalent is spent making H2 gas and the carboxylate.

steps.label: Hydride from another AlH4⁻ adds to the carboxylate carbon
One oxygen bonds to aluminum (AlH3), making it a leaving group
C=O reforms and the O–Al group leaves, giving an aldehyde
steps.note: The aldehyde is more reactive than the starting material, so it is reduced at once.

steps.label: A further hydride adds to the aldehyde carbonyl carbon
Acid workup protonates the alkoxide

why: LiAlH4 first deprotonates the acid (H2 gas is released), then hydride reduces the aluminum carboxylate through an aldehyde stage that is reduced again at once. Workup gives the 1° alcohol; NaBH4 is too weak to reduce a carboxylic acid.

traps.explains: LiAlH4 doesn't stop at the aldehyde; the aldehyde is more reactive than the acid and is reduced right away.
No reaction would be NaBH4, which can't reduce carboxylic acids. LiAlH4 (or BH3) can.
Reduction stops at the alcohol. LiAlH4 does not remove the C–O bond to give a CH3 group.

review: Mechanism simplified (course-dependent): after the acid-base step the carboxylate and the tetrahedral dianion are drawn as free anions; real intermediates are O-Al aluminates. Product and reagent are correct.

title: RMgX + CO2 → carboxylic acid

steps.label: The Grignard carbon adds to the carbon of CO2
steps.note: CO2 is just a C=O electrophile with no leaving group, so it stops at the carboxylate salt.

steps.label: Acid workup protonates the carboxylate
steps.note: The two carboxylate oxygens are equivalent by resonance, so it doesn't matter which one takes the proton.

why: The Grignard carbon adds to the electrophilic carbon of CO2, forming a new C–C bond and a magnesium carboxylate. The negatively charged carboxylate doesn't react with more Grignard, and H3O+ workup protonates it to the carboxylic acid with one more carbon.

traps.explains: The magnesium carboxylate is negatively charged and not electrophilic, so a second Grignard doesn't add.
That's what water does to a Grignard (protonation). Here CO2 is added first; water only comes in the workup.
The carboxylate is what's present after step 1. H3O+ workup protonates it to benzoic acid.

distractors.explains: Aryl halides don't undergo SN2, so cyanide can't displace the bromide and no nitrile forms to hydrolyze.
LiAlH4 reduces the ester to benzyl alcohol; it can't stop at, or form, the carboxylic acid.

title: Carboxylic acid + RMgX → acid–base only (trap)

steps.label: The Grignard's carbon acts as a base and removes the acidic O–H proton
steps.note: Acid–base is much faster than addition; CH4 bubbles off and the carboxylate is too unreactive to attack.

steps.label: Acid workup protonates the carboxylate, giving back the starting acid

why: A Grignard is a very strong base, so it simply removes the acidic O–H proton and becomes methane; no C–C bond forms. The carboxylate salt is negatively charged and not electrophilic enough for the Grignard to add, so H3O+ workup just gives back the starting acid.

traps.explains: The Grignard never adds to the C=O: it is destroyed by the acidic O–H first, and the carboxylate left behind is not electrophilic. (Ketones from acids need 2 equiv of an organolithium.)
Adding twice is what happens with an ester, which has no acidic proton. An acid just protonates the Grignard.
The carboxylate (as its MgBr⁺ salt) is what forms in step 1, but H3O+ workup protonates it back to the carboxylic acid.

review: Product is drawn as the recovered starting acid (after H3O+ workup), with methane as the byproduct; the carboxylate salt is a trap. Check the app copes with a product identical to the reactant, and whether you'd rather make the answer the carboxylate salt (drop step 2). Pattern set to X (acid–base, not acyl substitution); key step is proton transfer from O–H to the Grignard carbon, with the H drawn explicitly.

title: Ester + NH3 → amide (aminolysis)

steps.label: Ammonia attacks the ester carbonyl carbon
The tetrahedral intermediate collapses: C=O reforms and methoxide leaves
Methoxide removes a proton from the nitrogen
steps.note: The amide is much more stable than the ester, which is what makes this direction downhill.

why: Ammonia attacks the ester carbonyl and methoxide leaves (then grabs a proton to become methanol). Ester → amide is a step down the reactivity ladder, so it is favorable, but esters are much less reactive than acid chlorides, so it is slower and usually needs heat.

traps.explains: That's hydrolysis by water. Here NH3 is the nucleophile, so nitrogen ends up on the carbonyl.
This is the tetrahedral intermediate (after proton transfer). It collapses: the C=O re-forms and methoxide, the leaving group, is expelled.
Ammonium acetate would need acetic acid to deprotonate. An ester has no acidic O–H; NH3 adds to the C=O instead.

title: Anhydride + alcohol → ester

steps.label: Methanol attacks one carbonyl carbon of the anhydride
The tetrahedral intermediate collapses: C=O reforms and acetate leaves
steps.note: Acetate is a good leaving group (weak base), so anhydrides are nearly as reactive as acid chlorides.

steps.label: Pyridine removes the proton from the oxonium oxygen

why: Methanol attacks one carbonyl of the anhydride and acetate (a good, resonance-stabilized leaving group) leaves. Anhydride → ester is down the reactivity ladder; the byproduct is a carboxylic acid instead of the HCl an acid chloride would give.

traps.explains: This is the tetrahedral intermediate. It collapses, re-forming C=O and expelling acetate, a good leaving group.
The alcohol attacks through oxygen, so no C–C bond forms. A ketone would need a carbon nucleophile.
No reaction is wrong: anhydrides are above esters on the reactivity ladder, so an alcohol converts them to an ester readily.
